answers.note: Clear five-step process with a coverage table, traffic-light summary and ordered actions, but its reference list puts things that are not in the KS3 programme of study (judging search ranking, copyright) under the national curriculum and skips text, sound and image representation.

Thorough and accurate: coded KS3 strands, lesson-level tagging with depth codes, a termly grid with example rows, progression-break analysis, team sense-checking and a prioritised action plan with owners and deadlines.

Strong, practical method with an accurate 22-point breakdown, an I/D/A/R grid with illustrative rows, explicit order and progression checks, and a ranked action list. One small slip: it says the programme of study has nine bullet points when it has ten.

Excellent plan that gives both sceptics a real role, includes an error hunt and hands-on generation for real upcoming content, sets out a six-step checking routine, and times out to exactly 45 minutes with a two-week trial and a review that ends in a decision.

Well-structured 45-minute agenda (sub-timings add up) that reframes each concern as a testable question, includes an error demo and 18 minutes of paired hands-on work with a checking protocol, and ends with a logged trial and a review date.

Tight and practical with hands-on work on teachers' own worksheets, but it calls all three colleagues sceptics, adds a worry nobody raised, reduces error checking to 'solve every question', and never separates teacher use from student use of AI.
Comprehensive and accurate on UK GDPR, inaccuracy, acceptable and unacceptable uses, and transparency, but at ten sections it is long for staff to follow, and the under-13s rule is unexplained.

Covers every criterion clearly, with practical anonymising and approved-account steps, a four-question checking routine, transparency with students and parents, and a ready-to-use one-paragraph handbook version.
Concise and practical on data protection, inaccuracy and testing a tool on essays already marked, but it never mentions being open with students or parents about AI use.
